title: The Two-Plate Reckoning
subtitle: Amen at 11:55. Ranch at 12:10.
credit: A Nathan Tabor / Nathan AI project

chapters.title: Hold Everything and Clear the Aisle
paras: At 11:55 the last amen still had a tail on it. By 12:10 the preacher was leaning over the sneeze guard like he had spotted the Promised Land in a pan of mashed potatoes. His wife had already counted the open tables, picked the one that left the aisle clear, and worked out how to reach the hot yeast rolls before the next batch of folks in Sunday suits.

This is a fictional Independent Fundamental Baptist (IFB) preacher, his wife, and a Sunday shift at an imaginary buffet. The portions are invented for the story and tracked in the game. The server accounts at the end come from published interviews and firsthand posts.
Two plates each. One check. The pulpit gets forty-five minutes. The receipt gets the last word.

chapters.title: The Preacher Stacks It
paras: Plate one carries two pieces of fried chicken, two scoops of mashed potatoes, one scoop of brown gravy, and one yeast roll. Six portions. He sets the chicken edgewise, banks the potatoes against it, and pours the gravy into the valley. He eats on a hot-first schedule and tears that roll in half to mop the plate.

Plate two carries two slices of roast beef, one scoop of mac and cheese, one yeast roll, one dish of banana pudding, and one scoop of peach cobbler. Six more portions. The meat goes down first, the bread sweeps up, and dessert gets whatever square inch survives. Twelve portions across the two plates.

He takes the first bite standing up because somebody wants to shake his hand. Then he sits and tells a story through three courses. Sweet tea is a refill request on the receipt. It has its own line because a glass still takes a trip.

chapters.title: The Preacher’s Wife Sets the Rim
paras: She goes through the same line with a different system. Plate one carries one slice of roast beef, one scoop of green beans, one scoop of mashed potatoes, one scoop of brown gravy, and one yeast roll. Five portions. She puts the gravy on the potatoes, sections off the beans, and eats one forkful from each side of the plate.

Plate two carries one piece of fried chicken, one scoop of mac and cheese, one yeast roll, and one scoop of peach cobbler. Four portions. She keeps the cobbler at the rim so it stays out of the chicken juices, and saves it for the last bite. Nine portions across two plates. Together they take twenty-one portions, with drinks counted separately.

She notices that the server has three other tables waving. She slides the empty glasses to the aisle side and asks for the two refills together. A perfectly arranged plate can still belong to a table that hands somebody a miserable shift. What she does next matters more.

chapters.title: The Fifteen-Top
paras: The ranch, the cornbread, the sweet tea. Three people ask on three different trips. A fourth holds up a glass from the far side of the table. Somewhere between the kitchen and the twelve other glasses the server is carrying, somebody decides two minutes is a personal insult.

Combine the requests and give the kitchen time. Pull the chair out of the aisle. When you fold that imitation bill under a plate, the person lifting it gets one second of relief before the joke lands. There is still rent on the other side of that joke.

When the check comes in the story, it reads $36.00 before tax. One plus one equals two. Twenty percent of $36.00 is $7.20. The play receipt counts real cash or card tips. It records the imitation bill as zero.

chapters.title: Who I Am. Whom I Be. What I Bee.
paras: John Nathan Tabor. Preacher’s kid. IFB. KJV. Youngest of three boys. Owens Cross Roads, Alabama, and the Flint River are where Nathan puts the beginning of this story. Hooked on Phonics, McGuffey Readers, the King James Bible, television, movies, and music. In his family telling, Grandma Opal’s line was to play dumb until you know what you’re dealing with.

“Well, whatca need done—and when you need it done by?” That is the question Nathan brings to the table. Who I am is the PK who knows the cadence. Whom I be is the one looking to see who did the work. What I bee is the honey and the stinger. The honey is giving freely. The stinger is reading the receipt out loud. INNOCENCE IS NOT A COMMODITY.
“MY YES IS MY YES. MY NO IS MY NO. 1 + 1 = 2!” Nathan’s twenty-percent rule gets a dollar line. That is where the person who carried the plates can see it.

chapters.title: The KJV at the Check
paras: Proverbs 23:20–21 puts riotous eating and gluttony on the page. James 5:4 makes withheld wages cry out. 1 Timothy 5:18 says, “The labourer is worthy of his reward.” James 1:27 puts care for the fatherless and widows in plain view.

The hard question belongs at your own table. How did you speak to the person pouring the tea? How many times did you send them back? Was the paper under the plate money? Who put the room back in order after you left?
The preacher’s wife puts the card down before the preacher can fish for a tract. He looks at the total, takes a beat, and writes $7.20. They clear the aisle on the way out.

chapters.title: Receipts From the Shift
paras: In a 2017 Christian Post opinion piece, Shane Pruitt printed accounts from servers who recalled demanding after-church tables, low tips and tracts left on the table. Jason Pierce’s essay draws on those same interviews. Treat the two articles as overlapping evidence.

In a 2019 r/Christianity discussion, a commenter recalled lower per-customer tips on Sundays while working as a server. Other commenters describe paper that looks like money. These accounts speak to individual experiences. The cited material gives neither a representative industry-wide ranking nor typical portion counts for IFB families.

U.S. Department of Labor Fact Sheet #15 describes the federal $2.13 direct cash wage where an employer lawfully uses a tip credit. The employer must make up a workweek shortfall against the applicable minimum. More protective state standards can apply.
